Machine Learning in Financial Risk Management

Machine Learning-Assisted Dynamic Risk Exposure

This presentation documents a walk-forward validated framework for converting Machine Learning signals into risk-managed exposure. The framework is asset-agnostic and has been evaluated across multiple stocks.

The strategy adjusts exposure dynamically using Machine Learning probabilities, trend filters, volatility controls, drawdown protection, early risk-on recovery logic, multiplicative sentiment scaling and turnover-aware rebalance controls. Sections 1-9 describe the current notebook methodology. Sections 10-13 present the specific results for the selected asset: AMZN with model Optuna tuned.

1. Research Objective

Does a validation-disciplined XGBoost probability model, translated by a deterministic exposure engine, improve risk-adjusted out-of-sample behavior relative to buy-and-hold?

The classifier does not predict the exact price or daily return. It estimates risk_on_proba = P(y_t = 1 | X_t), where y_t is a favorable future-return regime label based on a weighted future open-to-open return exceeding a train-derived threshold. The exposure engine converts this probability into target_position using trend, volatility, drawdown, sentiment and risk controls. The execution/backtest layer then applies a one-row delay, rebalance band, transaction costs, cash yield and leverage financing before comparing out-of-sample results with buy-and-hold.

Risk-First Evaluation

Assessment focuses on out-of-sample risk-adjusted behavior: Sharpe difference, drawdown, volatility, turnover, costs and annualized return.

General Asset Workflow

The workflow accepts a selected stock, ETF or liquid instrument. It builds ticker-based price, context, sentiment and filing/event features without hardcoded company assumptions.

Execution Assumptions

Signals trade through target_position.shift(1). The backtest includes a no-trade band, 5 bps per unit turnover, cash yield on unallocated capital and financing for exposure above 1.0.

ExplanationThe model estimates favorable-regime probability only. The deterministic engine decides exposure, and the final test evaluates whether that exposure path has better risk-adjusted out-of-sample behavior than passive buy-and-hold under the same timing and cost assumptions.

2. System Architecture

The system separates prediction, exposure construction, and execution/backtesting.

The classifier output is only a probability. A deterministic exposure layer maps risk_on_proba plus point-in-time market, risk and sentiment state into target_position. The execution layer applies delay, rebalance logic, transaction costs, cash return and leverage financing. This separation makes timing and tuning boundaries explicit and helps limit leakage and overfitting risk.

1
Data/context.
Daily OHLCV, warm-up history, cross-market variables, real-news sentiment and filing/event context are collected for the selected asset.
2
Point-in-time features.
Technical, volatility, volume, trend, sentiment and event features are aligned to after-close signal time. News and filing/event inputs are shifted one trading row.
3
Chronological split and labels.
Train, validation and test remain ordered in time. Labels use weighted future open-to-open returns and thresholds derived from the allowed training window.
4
Probability models.
Weighted XGBoost and an Optuna-tuned candidate estimate risk_on_proba = P(y_t = 1 | X_t). The output is a probability, not a trade.
5
Validation/walk-forward selection.
Model candidates are compared with walk-forward folds; exposure, sentiment and risk settings are selected on validation with train-only probabilities and locked before the final test.
6
Final test and metrics.
The selected probability path and locked engine settings are evaluated on the final holdout with net returns, drawdown, volatility, turnover, costs and buy-and-hold comparison metrics.

3. Data and Market Context

The dataset combines selected-asset OHLCV, classic technical indicators, cross-market context, and real-news sentiment/event context into one chronological feature table.

Primary prices come from daily Open/High/Low/Close/Volume fetched through Yahoo/yfinance for the selected asset. The notebook loads a 2-year warm-up period before the formal sample start so rolling indicators are stable, then keeps the modeling sample in chronological train, validation, and test order. There is no random split.

Technical Market State

Classic indicators describe trend, momentum, volatility, drawdown and volume pressure using returns/momentum over 1d, 3d, 5d, 10d and 20d windows, RSI and StochRSI, MACD / MACD-derived features, SMA/EMA trend features, VWMA, ATR, Bollinger width and realized-volatility features, drawdown from recent peaks, and volume or dollar-volume z-score/anomaly features.

Cross-Market Context

Macro and risk-regime inputs are aligned to the primary asset calendar, including VIX level, changes, spikes and above-moving-average flags, Treasury/rates proxy TNX, dollar index DXY, and ES/NQ/YM equity-index futures returns or momentum. These fields help separate asset-specific movement from broad market stress or risk-on/risk-off conditions.

Real-News Sentiment

Public headline sentiment is aggregated daily into compact features such as sentiment_ma_5d, sentiment_change_3d, sentiment_extremity, news_volume, news_volume_zscore, sentiment_confidence, and sentiment_has_news. No-news periods are neutral, not synthetic positive or negative sentiment. Raw daily sentiment and news volume are shifted one trading row before model use to avoid same-day news leakage. GDELT is one public source used for historical headline discovery, and source-query mechanics are not the focus of this section.

Compact Filing/Event Context

When available, SEC filings add small event-count features such as total filing count, 8-K count, 10-Q/10-K count, and days since filing. The notebook resolves public-company filings through CIK when available, shifts filing counts by one trading row, and leaves unavailable filing context neutral.

Data Quality and Preprocessing

Cross-market and context variables are forward-filled onto the primary asset's trading calendar. Later, model-matrix missingness is handled with train-split rules: columns with more than 10% missing values in train are dropped, and remaining train/validation/test feature gaps are filled with train means.

Leakage controlChronological splitting matters because random shuffling would mix future market regimes into training. News sentiment and SEC/event context are shifted one trading row, so same-day headlines or filings are not treated as tradable information for that row.

4. Feature Engineering

Features convert raw market, news, and event data into point-in-time variables available at signal time. They describe trend, momentum, volatility, stress, liquidity and volume, cross-market regime, sentiment, and filing/event context.

The timing convention is explicit. The model observes information after market close at time t, builds the feature row for that close, and the trading engine executes at the next market open. Technical and cross-market fields are aligned to the asset trading calendar. Sentiment inputs and SEC filing event inputs are shifted by one trading row before model use, so same-day news or filings are not treated as tradable information for that row. No-news and no-filing periods stay neutral rather than being converted into artificial positive or negative signals.

Trend and Momentum

Return and momentum features cover several horizons, including return_1d, return_3d, return_5d, return_10d, return_20d, return_40d, return_60d, mom_10_pct, and macd_pct. Oscillator features include centered RSI fields rsi_5_centered, rsi_10_centered, rsi_15_centered, plus normalized StochRSI. Trend distance and slope features include close_to_sma_5, close_to_sma_10, close_to_sma_20, close_to_ema_5, close_to_ema_10, close_to_ema_20, close_to_ema_50, close_to_ema_100, close_to_ema_200, ema_20_slope_3d, ema_50_slope_5d, ema_100_slope_5d, ema_200_slope_5d, ema_20_50_trend, and ema_50_200_trend.

Volatility and Stress

Volatility features normalize risk across price levels and time windows. The notebook uses atr_14_pct, bb_width_pct, bb_position, volatility_5d, volatility_20d, volatility_60d, volatility_ratio_5_20, and volatility_ratio_20_60. Stress fields include recent drawdown and gap behavior, such as drawdown_20d, drawdown_60d, overnight_gap, and gap_volatility_20d. These variables help distinguish normal trend movement from unstable or defensive market conditions.

Volume and Liquidity

Volume features describe participation, confirmation, and abnormal activity. Examples include volume_change_5d, volume_change_10d, volume_zscore_20, dollar_volume_zscore_20, obv_change_5d, ad_change_5d, and volume_price_confirmation. These features help the model separate moves with broad participation from weaker price changes that occur on low or unusual volume.

Cross-Market Regime

Context features describe whether the selected asset is moving with or against the wider market. VIX examples include vix_level, vix_change_3d, vix_change_5d, vix_close_return_1d, vix_close_return_3d, vix_close_return_5d, vix_close_return_20d, vix_ma_20, vix_above_ma_20, vix_spike_3d, and vix_spike_5d. Rates and dollar context include tnx_level, TNX changes, dxy_level, and DXY changes. Equity-index context uses ES, NQ, and YM returns or momentum, relative-strength fields such as rel_strength_es_20d, rel_strength_nq_20d, and rel_strength_ym_20d, plus combined regime fields trend_vix_risk and momentum_vix_risk.

Sentiment Layer

Public-news sentiment is collected under bounded request caps, aggregated by publication day, and shifted one trading row before model use. The compact feature set includes sentiment_daily, sentiment_ma_5d, sentiment_change_3d, sentiment_extremity, news_volume, news_volume_zscore, sentiment_confidence, and sentiment_has_news. When no usable news is available for a trading row, sentiment impact is neutral and distinguishable through the news-volume and has-news fields.

SEC Filing Events

SEC/event features add compact public filing context when it is available for the selected ticker. The model can use sec_filing_count, sec_8k_count, sec_10q_10k_count, sec_material_event_flag, sec_registration_count, sec_amendment_count, sec_days_since_filing, and sec_data_available. Filing counts are mapped to the trading calendar and shifted one trading row, while unavailable SEC data remains neutral.

Feature Selection and Importance

After feature construction, the model matrix is filtered using training-split information only. Features with excessive missingness in the training split are removed, remaining train, validation, and test gaps are filled with train means, and correlation clustering removes redundant features with pairwise correlation above 0.82. The final feature count is asset/run-dependent because availability, missingness, and correlation structure vary by run. SHAP then explains how the final model uses the selected features.

signal_time = market_close_t
features_t = technical_t + cross_market_t + lagged_sentiment_t + lagged_sec_events_t
execution_time = next_market_open

5. Target Construction And Chronological Split

The target is a binary label for a favorable future-return regime. It is not a raw price prediction and it is not a direct prediction of the next close.

The notebook uses an open-to-open target because the trading workflow acts at the next session open. A feature row is built from information available after the close at time t. The executable entry is therefore Open.shift(-1), matching the engine's next-session execution timing.

The notebook first splits df_ta chronologically into train (earliest 60%), validation (next 20%), and test (final 20%). It then calls add_future_return_target() inside each split separately to compute future_return and target. This ordering prevents future-return boundary leakage across train, validation, and test.

Labels are based on a weighted blend of 3-day, 5-day, and 10-day open-to-open forward returns. Because the future returns are computed inside each chronological split or walk-forward fold, rows near split boundaries are labeled only with data available inside that split. Rows where the required future open is unavailable become NaN and are dropped from the labeled set.

for horizon in [3, 5, 10]:
    entry_price = Open.shift(-1)
    exit_price = Open.shift(-(horizon + 1))
    future_return_h = exit_price / entry_price - 1

future_return = (
    0.40 * future_return_3d
    + 0.35 * future_return_5d
    + 0.25 * future_return_10d
)

long_threshold = train_df["future_return"].quantile(0.60)
target = (future_return > long_threshold).astype(int)

Binarization Threshold

The main split sets long_threshold = train_df["future_return"].quantile(0.60). The 0.60 quantile is a manual research/design choice, not a threshold learned automatically by the model. It defines target=1 as roughly the top 40% of training future-return outcomes, with target=0 for the remaining outcomes.

The same train-derived threshold is then applied to train, validation, and test labels in the main split. Validation and test rows do not set their own threshold. When the final model is refit, it uses train + validation labeled data and computes its 0.60 threshold from train + validation only, the test set still does not set the threshold. In walk-forward evaluation, the notebook uses WF_TARGET_QUANTILE = 0.60 and recomputes the threshold using each fold's training subset only.

Leakage controlThere is no target leakage from this construction. The threshold uses only the past/training return distribution. Future returns are labels, not model features. Split-edge rows are labeled inside their own split, and rows without enough future open prices are dropped before modeling.

6. Machine Learning Models

The machine-learning layer estimates the probability of a favorable future-return regime. It does not produce a direct buy/sell instruction and it does not forecast the exact future price.

For each trading day t, the model receives X_t, a feature vector built from the technical, volatility, volume, cross-market, sentiment, and event variables described above. It learns from the binary label y_t in (0, 1) constructed in Section 5. The model output is risk_on_proba = P(y_t = 1 | X_t), interpreted as the estimated probability that the next labeled horizon belongs to the favorable regime.

Model Mechanism

XGBoost is an additive ensemble of decision trees. Each tree contributes a small function of the current feature vector, and the raw model score is the sum of those tree contributions.

score(X_t) = sum_k f_k(X_t)

The raw score is then mapped to a probability through the logistic sigmoid function.

risk_on_proba = sigma(score) = 1 / (1 + exp(-score))

The sigmoid transforms any real-valued score into the interval [0,1], so large positive scores imply high estimated risk-on probability and large negative scores imply low estimated risk-on probability.

Training Objective

The classifier is trained with binary log loss, which penalizes confident wrong probabilities more strongly than uncertain errors.

L = -[y log(p) + (1-y) log(1-p)]

Regularization, restricted tree complexity, sample weighting, and chronological validation/model selection keep the tree ensemble from fitting noise too closely. This is especially important in financial data, where excessive model complexity can produce overconfident probabilities that do not generalize out of sample.

Class Imbalance

The 0.60 target threshold creates a roughly 60/40 label split, so one class is usually less frequent than the other. Balanced sample weights are used so the model does not ignore whichever class is minority in a given split, whether favorable or unfavorable. The goal is not to maximize naive accuracy, but to learn both sides of the risk-on/risk-off distinction.

Weighted XGBoost Baseline

The weighted XGBoost baseline is a fixed reference model. It uses balanced sample weights, restricted tree complexity, and regularization to estimate risk_on_proba without a broad search over alternative model and trading settings. Its role is to provide a robust benchmark: if a more complex candidate does not clearly improve the trading usefulness of the probability path, the baseline remains the safer reference.

Optuna-Tuned Candidate

The Optuna-tuned XGBoost model is a candidate, not an automatic replacement for the baseline. The notebook uses a TPE sampler and runs study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50). Each trial samples alternative XGBoost hyperparameters plus simple trading/exposure parameters: decision_threshold, low_exposure, high_exposure, risk_off_exposure, risk_on_boost, rebalance_threshold, and fast_vol_threshold.

The purpose is not to declare that Optuna is better because it searched more settings. The purpose is to test whether an alternative probability path is more useful for trading after basic exposure rules are applied.

Preliminary Trading Score

The 50 Optuna trials are evaluated with score_probability_strategy_next_open(), not with the full run_stock_strategy_backtest() Dynamic Exposure Engine explained in Section 7. This keeps model/signal selection separate from full portfolio and risk construction.

The mini scorer follows a simple causal flow: risk_on_proba is converted into a simple target_exposure, the exposure is shifted into an executable next-open position, open-to-next-open strategy returns are computed, and a compact trading score is assigned.

score = Sharpe + 0.25*Sortino + 0.70*Annualized Return - drawdown_penalty - turnover_penalty
drawdown_penalty = 0.80 * abs(max_drawdown)
turnover_penalty = 0.003 * total_turnover

This step avoids judging models by accuracy alone. It asks whether the probability sequence can support a tradable exposure path before adding the full Section 7 risk engine complexity.

Bridge to the Dynamic Exposure Engine

Section 6 selects and compares probability-producing models: the weighted baseline and the Optuna-tuned candidate. Section 7 then explains the full Dynamic Exposure Engine that converts the selected probabilities into final target_position with exposure limits, transaction-cost-aware rebalancing, defensive risk controls, and portfolio-level execution logic.

Why XGBoost?

XGBoost is a robust tabular model for noisy, mixed financial features. It captures nonlinear effects and feature interactions without requiring very large datasets, works well with modest sample sizes, supports regularization and constrained tree structure, and is compatible with SHAP-based interpretation. These properties make it a suitable academic baseline for technical, cross-market, sentiment, and event features.

Model Comparison SummaryThe weighted XGBoost baseline is the reference. The Optuna-tuned variant is accepted only if validation or walk-forward evidence shows that its probability path improves the downstream trading objective without excessive overfitting. In both cases, the model outputs probability only, the risk engine decides the final exposure.

7. Dynamic Exposure Engine

The Weighted XGBoost baseline gives one probability path, p_t^W. The Optuna-tuned candidate gives another probability path, p_t^O. Each value says how likely the model thinks day t belongs to a favorable future-return regime. Both paths then go through the exact same exposure and backtest rules, so the comparison is fair: only the probability path changes, not the trading engine.

p_t^W -> engine -> metrics_W     p_t^O -> engine -> metrics_O

The engine is not another Machine Learning model. It is a fixed set of portfolio rules. It takes the candidate probability p_t, the market information available at that time Z_t, and the locked settings θ. It outputs the desired exposure target_position, the actually held position, net returns, equity curves, drawdowns and final metrics.

Variable Glossary: Plain Meaning, Source And Use

1) Model / Probability

VariableRole and origin
risk_on_proba / p_tThe model probability for day t, created by predict_proba(X_t)[:, 1]. In simple terms, it is the model's estimate of P(y_t=1 | X_t): how likely the future-return label is favorable.
lower_thresholdThe low probability reference point. It helps turn the raw probability into a usable exposure signal. If not supplied, the engine uses the 0.30 quantile of the probability path given to it.
upper_thresholdThe high probability reference point. If not supplied, the engine uses the 0.70 quantile of the probability path given to it.
X_train_validationThe training-split feature matrix used by the train-only validation_model for validation-safe threshold tuning.
train_validation_proba_seriesvalidation_model.predict_proba(X_train_validation)[:, 1] (same idea as train-only X_train probabilities). Candidate numeric thresholds come from this series using (0.30,0.70), (0.35,0.70) and (0.30,0.65), are judged on validation, and are frozen before test.
proba_rangemax(upper_threshold - lower_threshold, 1e-9). This is the usable distance between the two thresholds. The tiny 1e-9 floor avoids division by zero.
probability_tiltThe model's exposure push, centered between [-model_tilt, +model_tilt]. A low p_t reduces exposure, a high p_t increases exposure.
model_tiltThe maximum positive or negative exposure change that the model probability is allowed to make.

2) Base Exposure / Trend

VariableRole and origin
base_exposureThe starting risky-asset allocation before the model probability, trend filter and risk controls change it.
trend_onThe long-term trend flag. It first checks close_to_ema_200 > 0, if missing, it checks price > ema_200, if both are missing, it stays neutral/on as True.
trend_bonusThe exposure add-on when trend_on=1.
trend_penaltyThe exposure reduction when trend_on=0.
trend_adjustmentThe trend contribution used inside raw_exposure: +trend_bonus when trend_on=1, and -trend_penalty when trend_on=0.
raw_exposureThe first exposure estimate before risk controls: base_exposure + probability_tilt + trend_adjustment.

3) Volatility / Risk Multipliers

VariableRole and origin
market_returnThe return that the held position earns from one open to the next open: Open.shift(-1) / Open - 1. The last unavailable value is filled with 0.
past_open_returnPast open-to-open returns from Open.pct_change(fill_method=None). These are used only to estimate recent volatility.
realized_vol_20dpast_open_return.rolling(20).std().shift(1) * sqrt(252). This is yesterday-known 20-day annualized volatility, shift(1) prevents using the return being measured today.
target_volThe desired volatility level used in target_vol / realized_vol_20d.
vol_floorThe lower limit for the volatility multiplier, so volatility control does not cut exposure too far only because volatility changed.
vol_ceilingThe upper limit for the volatility multiplier, so volatility control does not raise exposure too far only because volatility changed.
vol_multiplierclip(target_vol / realized_vol_20d, vol_floor, vol_ceiling), filled with 1.0 when missing. It cuts exposure in high volatility and can raise it in low volatility.
vix_levelThe VIX market-stress level available in the feature set.
vix_ma_20The 20-day VIX average when vix_level exists.
vix_risk_multiplierThe defensive multiplier used when prior vix_level is above prior vix_ma_20.
vix_multiplierExact rule: vix_multiplier = vix_risk_multiplier when vix_level.shift(1) > vix_ma_20.shift(1), otherwise it is 1.0.
rolling_high_60dThe recent 60-day high used to measure drawdown.
drawdown_60dThe current loss from the recent high. The equation is drawdown_60d = Close.shift(1) / rolling_high_60d.shift(1) - 1, so it uses only prior close information.
drawdown_cutoffThe drawdown level that marks a defensive state.
drawdown_risk_multiplierThe defensive multiplier used when shifted 60-day drawdown is worse than the cutoff.
drawdown_multiplierExact rule: drawdown_multiplier = drawdown_risk_multiplier when drawdown_60d < drawdown_cutoff, otherwise it is 1.0.

4) Defensive / Offensive Overlays

VariableRole and origin
risk_off_exposureThe maximum exposure allowed when trend_on == 0 and p_t < lower_threshold, and again when fast_risk_off == 1.
fast_vol_thresholdThe volatility-ratio cutoff used by the quick danger check.
fast_conditionsThe available quick danger inputs: close_to_ema_20 < 0, return_5d < 0, and volatility_ratio_5_20 > fast_vol_threshold.
fast_risk_scoreThe number of active quick danger inputs. Exact rule: fast_risk_score = sum(condition.astype(int) for condition in fast_conditions). If no conditions exist, score is 0.
fast_risk_offThe defensive flag from the quick danger score. Exact rule: fast_risk_off = fast_risk_score >= min(2, len(fast_conditions)). If no conditions exist, it is False.
risk_on_boostAn extra exposure add-on when p_t >= upper_threshold, trend_on == 1, close_to_ema_20 > 0, and fast_risk_off == 0.
recovery_risk_onA recovery flag. Exact conditions: strong_risk_on == True, return_20d > 0, and return_5d > 0.
recovery_min_exposureThe exposure floor used when recovery_risk_on is active.
strong_bull_regimeA stronger bullish state. Exact conditions: recovery_risk_on == True, return_60d > 0, drawdown_20d > -0.08, and volatility_ratio_5_20 < fast_vol_threshold.
bull_min_exposureThe exposure floor used when strong_bull_regime is active.
leveraged_bull_regimeThe most aggressive bullish state. Exact conditions: strong_bull_regime == True, return_20d > 0.05, and return_60d > 0.08.
bull_leverage_exposureThe exposure floor used when leveraged_bull_regime is active.
early_risk_on_scoreThe early recovery score: count(True) across close_to_ema_20 > 0, ema_20_slope_3d > 0, return_5d > 0, return_3d_minus_10d > 0, return_5d_minus_20d > 0, volatility_ratio_5_20 < fast_vol_threshold, and optional vix_change_5d < 0.
early_risk_on_score_thresholdThe minimum early recovery score needed to activate the flag. Default threshold is 4.
early_risk_onThe early recovery flag. Exact rule: early_risk_on = (early_risk_on_score >= early_risk_on_score_threshold) & (df_bt["fast_risk_off"] == 0).
early_risk_on_boostThe extra exposure added by np.where when early_risk_on is active.
early_recovery_min_exposureThe exposure floor applied by np.where when early_risk_on is active.

5) Sentiment

VariableRole and origin
sentiment_ma_5dA lagged 5-day real-news sentiment average from the feature pipeline. It is not synthetic. If there is no news, sentiment stays neutral.
sentiment_change_3dA lagged 3-day real-news sentiment change from the feature pipeline.
sentiment_score_rawThe raw news score: 0.70*sentiment_ma_5d + 0.30*sentiment_change_3d. It becomes 0.0 when no news exists.
sentiment_score_scaledThe bounded news score: tanh(sentiment_score_raw * sentiment_sensitivity). This keeps extreme sentiment bounded.
news_volumeThe number of headlines. It helps decide how much confidence to give the sentiment reading.
news_volume_zscoreA flag-like volume signal showing whether headline volume is unusually high.
sentiment_confidence_headlinesThe headline-count scale used when computing sentiment confidence.
sentiment_news_z_thresholdThe high-news-volume threshold that can add 0.25 to confidence.
sentiment_confidenceExact rule: if has_news, use clip(clip(news_volume / max(sentiment_confidence_headlines, 1e-9), 0, 1) + 0.25*(news_volume_zscore > sentiment_news_z_threshold), 0, 1), otherwise use 0.0.
sentiment_positive_max_adjustmentThe maximum positive exposure adjustment from sentiment.
sentiment_negative_max_adjustmentThe maximum negative exposure adjustment from sentiment before asymmetry.
sentiment_asymmetric_factorThe factor applied to negative sentiment, so bad news can be treated differently from good news.
sentiment_whipsaw_daysThe persistence rule: whipsaw_ok = (sentiment_dir == 0) | (cons_days >= sentiment_whipsaw_days), where sentiment_dir = sign(sentiment_score_scaled).
sentiment_regime_gateWhen active, composite fear is (vix_multiplier < 1.0) + (volatility_ratio_5_20 > 1.5) + (drawdown_60d < -0.10) >= 2. It sets positive sentiment multipliers above 1.0 back to 1.0, in strong_bull_regime == 1, negative multipliers are floored at 0.97.
sentiment_multiplierThe final sentiment exposure multiplier. No-news rows and whipsaw-filtered rows use multiplier 1.0.
sentiment_adjustmentThe distance of sentiment_multiplier from 1.0.

6) Execution / Costs

VariableRole and origin
min_exposureThe lowest exposure allowed after controls and clipping.
max_exposureThe highest exposure allowed after controls and clipping.
target_positionThe desired exposure after model probability, trend, risk controls, overlays and sentiment. It is clipped between min_exposure and max_exposure, and the fast-risk-off cap is reapplied after clipping.
executable_target_positiontarget_position.shift(1).fillna(base_exposure). This is yesterday's target, used as today's tradable target, so there is no same-row trading.
rebalance_thresholdThe no-trade band. The engine changes exposure only when abs(target - current_position) >= rebalance_threshold.
recovery_step_up_limitThe maximum size of a below-base upward recovery step. It does not cap bullish/risk-on targets at base_exposure, it only makes movement toward higher targets gradual. Downward defensive moves are not capped.
current_positionThe previous exposure used in the rebalance loop.
positionThe actually held exposure after execution delay and rebalance threshold.
turnoverThe trading amount: turnover = abs(diff(position)).
cost_bpsThe cost setting in basis points.
transaction_costcost_bps / 10000. Cost is charged per unit of turnover.
cash_yieldThe annual cash-yield setting for capital not invested in the risky asset.
cash_weightThe cash allocation: cash_weight = clip(1 - position, lower=0).
leverage_financing_rateThe financing-rate setting used when exposure is above 1.0.
leverage_amountThe exposure above 1.0: leverage_amount = clip(position - 1, lower=0).
financing_costThe daily cost charged for leverage_amount.
strategy_return_gross, strategy_return_netGross return adds risky-asset return and cash yield, then subtracts leverage financing. Net return additionally subtracts turnover cost.

7) Outputs / Metrics

OutputMeaning
strategy_equity, buy_hold_equityThe compounded value of the strategy and the passive buy-and-hold benchmark.
strategy_drawdown, buy_hold_drawdownHow far each equity curve is below its own previous peak.
Sharpe, Sortino, CalmarRisk-adjusted summaries based on daily net returns, downside daily returns and maximum drawdown.
Profit Factor, Win RateProfit Factor is gross positive daily net return divided by absolute gross negative daily net return. Win Rate is the share of days with positive net return.
Max Drawdown, Total Turnover, Average ExposureSimple diagnostics: worst peak-to-trough loss, total trading activity, and average risk exposure actually held.
Rebalance Days, Average Daily TurnoverRebalance Days counts days with turnover > 0. Average Daily Turnover is mean(turnover).
Fast Risk-Off Days, Early Risk-On DaysCounts of days when the fast defensive overlay or early recovery overlay is active. The notebook also reports Average Early Risk-On Score.
Strong Bull Days, Leveraged DaysStrong Bull Days counts rows where strong_bull_regime is active. Leveraged Days counts rows where the held position is above 1.0.
Average Leverage, Total Financing CostAverage Leverage is mean(leverage_amount), the average exposure above 1.0. Total Financing Cost is sum(financing_cost), the total daily cost charged for that leverage.
Sentiment diagnostics, if presentReported sentiment fields include Sentiment Risk-On Days, Sentiment Risk-Off Days, Average Sentiment Multiplier, Whipsaw Filtered Days and Average Sentiment Adjustment.

Timing And No-Leakage Discipline

The target exposure is computed after the close using only features and probabilities available for that row. The executable target is the prior row's target, target_position.shift(1).fillna(base_exposure). The measured return is market_return = Open.shift(-1) / Open - 1, with the final unavailable row filled by 0. So the engine cannot use the same row's open-to-next-open return to choose the position that earns that return. Volatility uses shifted past open returns, VIX stress uses prior VIX versus prior VIX moving average, and drawdown uses shifted close versus shifted rolling high.

Key Equations: Signal, Sentiment, Execution And Costs

The equations below show the main flow. Sentiment and execution/cost details stay inside the same code box because they are part of the same target-position and backtest process.

1) Signal
p_t = P(y_t=1 | X_t)

probability_tilt_t = (2*clip((p_t-L)/(U-L), 0, 1) - 1) * model_tilt
raw_exposure_t = base_exposure + probability_tilt_t + trend_adjustment_t

target_position_t = raw_exposure_t * vol_multiplier_t * vix_multiplier_t * drawdown_multiplier_t
target_position_t = apply_trend_cap_fast_risk_off_cap_and_bull_recovery_overlays(target_position_t)

2) Sentiment Mechanism
has_news_t = news_volume_t > 0
sentiment_score_raw_t = 0.70*sentiment_ma_5d_t + 0.30*sentiment_change_3d_t
sentiment_score_raw_t = where(has_news_t, sentiment_score_raw_t, 0.0)

sentiment_score_scaled_t = tanh(sentiment_score_raw_t * sentiment_sensitivity)

base_confidence_t = clip(news_volume_t / max(sentiment_confidence_headlines, 1e-9), 0, 1)
high_news_bonus_t = 0.25 * (news_volume_zscore_t > sentiment_news_z_threshold)
sentiment_confidence_t = where(
    has_news_t,
    clip(base_confidence_t + high_news_bonus_t, 0, 1),
    0.0,
)

sentiment_dir_t = sign(sentiment_score_scaled_t)
streak_id_t = cumulative_sum(sentiment_dir_t != sentiment_dirt-1)
consecutive_same_direction_days_t = group_count(streak_id_t) + 1
whipsaw_ok_t = (sentiment_dir_t == 0) | (consecutive_same_direction_days_t >= sentiment_whipsaw_days)

pos_limit = sentiment_positive_max_adjustment
neg_limit = sentiment_negative_max_adjustment * sentiment_asymmetric_factor

pos_scale_t = clip(sentiment_score_scaled_t, lower=0) * sentiment_confidence_t * pos_limit
neg_scale_t = clip(sentiment_score_scaled_t, upper=0) * sentiment_confidence_t * neg_limit

raw_mult_t = 1.0 + pos_scale_t + neg_scale_t
mult_t = where(has_news_t & whipsaw_ok_t, raw_mult_t, 1.0)

composite_fear_t = ((vix_multiplier_t < 1.0) + (volatility_ratio_5_20_t > 1.5) + (drawdown_60d_t < -0.10)) >= 2
mult_t = where(composite_fear_t & (mult_t > 1.0), 1.0, mult_t)

mult_t = where(strong_bull_regime_t & (mult_t < 1.0), maximum(mult_t, 0.97), mult_t)

sentiment_multiplier_t = where(has_news_t, mult_t, 1.0)
sentiment_adjustment_t = sentiment_multiplier_t - 1.0
sentiment_whipsaw_active_t = (~whipsaw_ok_t).astype(int)
sentiment_risk_on_t = sentiment_multiplier_t > 1.0
sentiment_risk_off_t = sentiment_multiplier_t < 1.0

target_position_t = target_position_t * sentiment_multiplier_t
target_position_t = where(fast_risk_off_t == 1, minimum(target_position_t, risk_off_exposure), target_position_t)

3) Execution / Costs
target_position_t = reapply_fast_risk_off_cap_clip_and_reapply_cap(target_position_t)
executable_target_position_t = target_positiont-1
position_t = rebalance_to_executable_target_only_when_band_is_exceeded(
    executable_target_position_t,
    positiont-1,
    rebalance_threshold,
    recovery_step_up_limit,
)

turnover_t = abs(position_t - positiont-1)
cash_weight_t = clip(1 - position_t, lower=0)
leverage_amount_t = clip(position_t - 1, lower=0)
financing_cost_t = leverage_amount_t * ((1 + leverage_financing_rate) ** (1/252) - 1)
turnover_cost_t = turnover_t * cost_bps / 10000
strategy_return_net_t = position_t * market_return_t + cash_weight_t * daily_cash_return_t - financing_cost_t - turnover_cost_t
strategy_equity_t = cumprod(1 + strategy_return_net_t)
strategy_drawdown_t = strategy_equity_t / running_max(strategy_equity_t) - 1

Daily Algorithm For Trading Day t

  1. After the close, receive p_t = P(y_t=1 | X_t), the point-in-time features, and the locked settings.
  2. Convert the probability into a centered exposure signal between negative and positive model_tilt.
  3. Add the trend effect and create the first exposure estimate.
  4. Scale exposure by known risk state: shifted realized volatility, prior VIX stress and shifted 60-day drawdown.
  5. Apply defensive and offensive overlays: trend-off cap, fast-risk-off cap, strong risk-on boost, recovery floor, strong-bull floor, leveraged-bull floor and early-risk-on boost/floor. Fast-risk-off is applied again after overlays.
  6. Apply real-news sentiment only when the overlay is active and real news exists. Then reapply the fast-risk-off cap, clip to [min_exposure, max_exposure], and reapply fast-risk-off once more so clipping cannot weaken the defensive cap.
  7. Delay execution. The target computed after the close becomes tomorrow's executable_target_position through target_position.shift(1). There is no same-row execution.
  8. Rebalance only if the executable target differs from current_position by at least rebalance_threshold. If held exposure is below base_exposure and the target is higher, recovery_step_up_limit caps only the step size toward the target, it does not cap risk-on targets at base_exposure. Downward defensive moves and existing above-base behavior are unchanged. Otherwise keep the previous position.
  9. Compute open-to-next-open return, turnover, cash yield, leverage financing, transaction costs, net return, equity, drawdown and metrics.
Final interpretationThe classifier supplies p_t. The deterministic exposure/backtest process turns it into tradable portfolio exposure. Because p_t^W and p_t^O use the same timing, risk, sentiment, cost and metric rules, the final comparison asks a clean question: which probability path is more useful after realistic portfolio translation?

8. Walk-Forward Model Selection and Validation-Safe Tuning

The current notebook compares a weighted XGBoost baseline with an optional Optuna-tuned XGBoost candidate over the chronological train + validation region. Each fold trains only on past observations, predicts the next unseen block, computes probability thresholds from fold-training probabilities, and evaluates fixed preliminary/default exposure rules on the evaluation block. Risk/exposure settings, fast-risk-off controls, early-risk-on behavior and sentiment settings are chosen later with a train-only validation model before final testing, the final test is not used for tuning.

What Is Walk-Forward Validation?

Walk-forward validation simulates a deployment-like research setting: train on past data, predict the next unseen period, then roll forward and repeat. This is fundamentally different from a single train/test split because it tests the model across multiple regime changes (bull markets, bear markets, consolidation periods). If a strategy performs well across all walk-forward folds but poorly on the final test, it may indicate overfitting to the validation period - a red flag that a single split would miss.

The notebook uses an expanding window approach: each fold trains on all available past data (the training set grows over time). Expanding windows are chosen here for regime detection because more training data may help the model learn recurring patterns, sliding windows are a valid alternative when older regimes should be down-weighted. The tradeoff is higher computational cost as the dataset grows.

Current notebook disciplineThe notebook separates model selection, validation-safe risk/exposure tuning, early-risk-on tuning, sentiment tuning and final testing. Risk/exposure templates are selected first, early-risk-on templates are validation-selected second and merged into selected_risk_settings, then sentiment templates are selected. Early-risk-on remains gated by fast_risk_off == 0, and the fast-risk-off defensive cap can override it. A train-only validation_model is used for validation tuning, while the final_model is trained on train + validation only after all selected settings are locked.

Current Walk-Forward Variables

VariableRole in the protocol
WF_FOLD_TEST_DAYSEvaluation fold length, currently 63 trading days (~1 quarter).
WF_FOLD_STEP_DAYSStep size between folds, currently 63 trading days (non-overlapping evaluations).
selection_rawChronological train + validation history used for walk-forward model comparison.
train_raw_foldExpanding past-only fold training window.
eval_raw_foldNext unseen chronological fold.
validation_modelModel trained on train only and used for honest validation risk/exposure tuning, including fast-risk-off and any early-risk-on overlay.
final_modelModel trained on train + validation after settings are locked, used for final test probabilities plus post-lock diagnostics/SHAP, not validation tuning.
selected_risk_settingsFrozen risk/exposure and sentiment configuration selected on validation, including fast-risk-off controls and any gated early-risk-on overlay.

Fold Logic

for each walk-forward fold:
    train_raw_fold = all rows before fold
    eval_raw_fold = next unseen block
    fit candidate model on train_raw_fold
    predict risk_on_proba on eval_raw_fold
    compute lower/upper thresholds from train probabilities only
    run dynamic exposure backtest with warm-up context
    store fold Sharpe, return, drawdown

Fold imputation values, target thresholds, probability thresholds and model fits are derived from training rows only. Evaluation rows never set their own thresholds. The 63-day fold length (~1 quarter of trading) aligns with quarterly re-evaluation cycles common in systematic trading. Folds are non-overlapping in evaluation, so there is no leakage between adjacent folds (no purging or embargo needed).

Threshold Computation: A Critical Leakage Prevention

A subtle but critical detail: lower_threshold and upper_threshold are computed from fold-training probabilities only. The evaluation fold never influences its own thresholds. If thresholds were computed on the full dataset (train + eval), the evaluation period would indirectly set the bar for its own risk-on/risk-off classification - a form of lookahead bias that inflates performance. The notebook prevents this by isolating training and evaluation data at every step of the pipeline.

Model Selection Logic

The walk-forward protocol always runs for the Weighted XGBoost baseline. It also runs for the Optuna-tuned candidate only when best_params / an Optuna candidate exists. Each available candidate produces a vector of fold-level Sharpe ratios. The model family with the higher mean Sharpe across folds is selected. If the baseline outperforms Optuna, or if no Optuna candidate exists, the simpler model wins. The selected model family then determines which final_model is trained on train+validation after settings are locked for the final test.

Validation-Safe Risk and Sentiment Tuning

After the model family is selected, the notebook trains a validation_model on the train split only. That model produces validation probabilities for separate validation-safe template passes: risk/exposure first, early-risk-on second, sentiment third. The selected early-risk-on parameters are merged into selected_risk_settings and evaluated with the selected risk/exposure controls, the overlay remains gated by fast_risk_off == 0, and an active fast-risk-off defensive cap overrides it. The winning selected_risk_settings are locked before the final_model is fit on train + validation. The final test is not used during this tuning step.

score = (
    Sharpe Ratio
    + 0.25 * Sortino Ratio
    + 0.50 * Annualized Return
    - 0.75 * abs(Max Drawdown)
    - 0.010 * Total_Turnover
)

This objective rewards risk-adjusted return, adds a smaller reward for downside-adjusted return and annualized return, and penalizes absolute drawdown plus turnover. It avoids selecting a high-return configuration that trades too often or creates excessive drawdown.

Validation-Safe Tuning Sequence

StepData usedPurpose
Model family selectionTrain + validation walk-forward foldsChoose Weighted XGBoost or Optuna XGBoost when the Optuna candidate exists.
validation_modelTrain onlyGenerate validation probabilities without fitting on validation labels.
Template tuningValidation onlySelect compact templates in sequence: risk/exposure controls first, validation-selected early-risk-on parameters second, sentiment settings third. Early-risk-on is evaluated with the selected risk/exposure controls, gated by fast_risk_off == 0, and overridden by fast-risk-off defensive caps.
selected_risk_settingsLocked after validationFreeze exposure-engine settings before final training.
final_modelTrain + validationFit after settings lock for final test plus post-lock diagnostics/SHAP, not validation tuning.

Final Test Discipline

After validation tuning, settings are locked and final metrics are computed on the untouched test window. The test set is not used to choose model parameters, risk/exposure templates, fast-risk-off controls, early-risk-on overlay settings, sentiment settings, probability/exposure thresholds, or turnover controls.

Why an Untouched Test Set Matters

Final-test settings are locked before the final test window is evaluated. The test set is never used for model selection, hyperparameter tuning, risk template tuning, early-risk-on parameter tuning, sentiment parameter tuning, or threshold computation. If you compare configurations using the test set, you are implicitly optimizing on it - even if you do not formally adjust parameters. The test set loses its value as an unbiased performance estimate once it influences research choices.

The pipeline enforces this discipline through two separate models: a validation_model trained on train only for separate validation passes over risk/exposure templates, early-risk-on templates and sentiment templates, and a separate final_model trained on train + validation only after those settings are locked. Final-test early-risk-on behavior uses the locked parameters inside the selected risk/exposure controls, remains gated by fast_risk_off == 0, and remains subject to fast-risk-off defensive override. The final_model supports final test measurement plus post-lock diagnostics/SHAP, not validation tuning. The test set never sees the validation model predictions, and the validation tuner never sees test set outcomes. This separation between validation-safe tuning and final evaluation is what distinguishes a research backtest from a validation-disciplined research workflow.

Why this mattersThe presentation reports a validation-disciplined research workflow: validation selects settings, final test measures them. Validation reuses a compact template set, so validation overfitting is still possible, there is no test leakage, and the final test remains the unbiased holdout.

9. Validation Discipline

Compact recap of the chronology that keeps target construction, tuning, walk-forward selection, final testing and diagnostics separated.

The main split is chronological 60/20/20: the earliest rows form train, the next block validation, and the final block test. The notebook first splits the feature table, then constructs future_return and target inside each split so labels do not cross split boundaries. During validation tuning, preprocessing choices, target-label thresholds, missing-value fills, the train-only validation_model, and probability/exposure threshold candidates come from training information only.

Validation Contract

Validation is used to choose compact model, risk, sentiment and overlay settings, it is not final performance evidence. The walk-forward protocol is an additional chronological check: each fold trains on past rows only, evaluates the next unseen block, uses preliminary/default exposure rules for candidate comparison, and includes the Optuna candidate only when best_params exists. After the model family and settings are locked, final_model is refit on train+validation labeled data only. The test window is then used only for final measurement, while SHAP is computed afterward as post-lock diagnostics rather than as a tuning signal.

What Each Split Is Allowed To Do

SplitAllowed useForbidden use
TrainFit preprocessing values, split-local labels, train-only validation model and training-derived threshold candidates.Report final performance.
ValidationSelect model family and compact risk, sentiment, probability/exposure threshold and early-risk-on settings.Measure final out-of-sample performance.
TestMeasure the locked strategy after final train+validation refit.Choose model, thresholds, overlays, rebalance settings or SHAP-based changes.
Why this mattersWalk-forward provides a stricter diagnostic than a single validation block because every fold respects time order. It does not guarantee robustness, and compact validation choices can still overfit the validation period. The locked final test therefore remains the primary holdout measurement, with SHAP reserved for interpretation after model and strategy choices are fixed.

10. SHAP interpretability

SHAP explains which features push the locked model toward risk-on or risk-off for AMZN.

SHAP decomposes final-model predictions into feature contributions. Positive SHAP values push a prediction toward risk-on, while negative values push it toward risk-off. The bar summary shows average absolute contribution, the summary plot shows the distribution over the explanation sample, and the binary SHAP plot separates risk-on and risk-off contribution patterns. These views are interpretation and diagnostics after model and strategy choices are fixed, not tuning inputs.
